{{Short description|Mathematical physics relation}}
In [[topology]] and [[high energy physics]], the '''Wu–Yang dictionary''' refers to the mathematical identification that allows  back-and-forth translation between the concepts of [[gauge theory]] and those of [[differential geometry]]. The dictionary appeared in 1975 in an article  by [[Tai Tsun Wu]] and [[Chen Ning Yang|C. N. Yang]] comparing [[electromagnetism]] and [[fiber bundle]] theory.<ref name=WUYangDictionary>{{Cite journal |last1=Wu |first1=Tai Tsun |last2=Yang |first2=Chen Ning |date=1975-12-15 |title=Concept of nonintegrable phase factors and global formulation of gauge fields |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.12.3845 |journal=Physical Review D |language=en |volume=12 |issue=12 |pages=3845–3857 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.12.3845 |issn=0556-2821|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This dictionary has been credited as bringing mathematics and [[theoretical physics]] closer together.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Poo |first1=Mu-ming |last2=Chao |first2=Alexander Wu |date=2020-01-01 |title=Conversation with Chen-Ning Yang: reminiscence and reflection |url=https://academic.oup.com/nsr/article/7/1/233/5544719 |journal=National Science Review |language=en |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=233–236 |doi=10.1093/nsr/nwz113 |issn=2095-5138 |pmc=8288855 |pmid=34692035}}</ref>

A crucial example of the success of the dictionary is that it allowed the understanding of [[Magnetic monopole#Dirac's quantization|monopole quantization]] in terms of [[Hopf fibration|Hopf fibrations]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Woit |first=Peter |date=5 April 2008 |title=Stony Brook Dialogues in Mathematics and Physics |url=https://www.math.columbia.edu/~woit/wordpress/?p=674 |access-date=2023-03-14 |website=Not even wrong blog |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Friedman |first=John L. |date=2015 |title=Historical note on fiber bundles |url=https://doi.org/10.1063/PT.3.2799 |journal=Physics Today |volume=68 |issue=6 |pages=11|doi=10.1063/PT.3.2799 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== History ==
Equivalences between fiber bundle theory and gauge theory were hinted at the end of the 1960s. In 1967, mathematician [[Andrzej Trautman]] started a series of lectures aimed at physicists and mathematicians at [[King's College London]] regarding these connections.<ref name=":1" />

Theoretical physicists [[Tai Tsun Wu]] and [[Chen Ning Yang|C. N. Yang]] working in [[Stony Brook University]], published a paper in 1975 on the mathematical framework of [[electromagnetism]] and the [[Aharonov–Bohm effect]] in terms of [[Fiber bundle|fiber bundles.]] A year later, mathematician [[Isadore Singer]] came to visit and brought a copy back to the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Wells |first1=Raymond O'Neil |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e0MECAAAQBAJ |title=The Mathematical Heritage of Hermann Weyl |last2=Weyl |first2=Hermann |date=1988 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. |isbn=978-0-8218-1482-6 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Freed |first=Daniel S. |date=2021 |title=Isadore Singer Transcended Mathematical Boundaries |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/isadore-singer-bridged-math-and-physics-20210304/ |website=Quanta Magazine}}</ref> Singer showed the paper to [[Michael Atiyah]] and other mathematicians, sparking a close collaboration between physicists and mathematicians.<ref name=":0" />

Yang also recounts a conversation that he had with one of the mathematicians that founded fiber bundle theory, [[Shiing-Shen Chern]]:<ref name=":0" />
{{Quote|text=In 1975, impressed with the fact that gauge fields are connections on fiber bundles, I drove to the house of Shiing-Shen Chern in [[El Cerrito, California|El Cerrito]], near [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]]. (I had taken courses with him in the early 1940s when he was a young professor and I an undergraduate student at the [[National Southwest Associated University]] in [[Kunming]], [[China]]. That was before fiber bundles had 
become important in differential geometry and before Chern had made history with his contributions to the generalized [[Gauss–Bonnet theorem]] and the [[Chern class]]es.) We had much to talk about: friends, relatives, China. When our conversation turned to fiber bundles, I told him that I had finally learned from [[Jim Simons]] the beauty of fiber-bundle theory and the profound [[Chern–Weil homomorphism|Chern-Weil theorem]]. I said I found it amazing that gauge fields are exactly connections on fiber bundles, which the mathematicians developed without reference to the physical world. I added ‘this is both thrilling and puzzling, since you mathematicians dreamed up these concepts out of nowhere.’ He immediately protested, ‘No, no. These concepts were not dreamed up. They were natural and real.'}}
In 1977, Trautman used these results to demonstrate an equivalence between a quantization condition for [[Magnetic monopole|magnetic monopoles]] used by [[Paul Dirac]] back in 1931 and [[Hopf fibration]], a fibration of a 3-sphere proposed in the same year by mathematician [[Heinz Hopf]].<ref name=":1" />
Mathematician [[Jim Simons]] discussing this equivalence with Yang expressed that “Dirac had discovered trivial and nontrivial bundles before mathematicians.”<ref name=":1" />

In the original paper, Wu and Yang added sources  (like the [[electric current]]) to the dictionary next to a blank spot, indicating a lack of any equivalent concept on the mathematical side. During interviews, Yang recalls that Singer and Atiyah found great interest in this concept of sources, which was unknown for mathematicians but that physicists knew since the 19th century. Mathematicians started working on that, which lead to the development of [[Donaldson theory]] by [[Simon Donaldson]], a student of Atiyah.<ref>{{Cite interview |last=Yang |first=C. N. |interviewer=Bill Zimmerman |title=C. N. Yang: Stony Brook Masters Series |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6d3hZ8jnqXg&ab_channel=StonyBrookUniversity |date=2009}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Wilson |first1=Robin |author-link=Robin Wilson (mathematician) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e0TTBwAAQBAJ&dq=wu+yang+dictionary+gauge+theory&pg=PA66 |title=Mathematical Conversations: Selections from The Mathematical Intelligencer |last2=Gray |first2=Jeremy |author-link2=Jeremy Gray (mathematician) |date=2012-12-06 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4613-0195-0 |language=en}}</ref>

== Description ==
=== Summarized version ===
The Wu-Yang dictionary relates terms in [[particle physics]] with terms in mathematics, specifically fiber bundle theory. Many versions and generalization of the dictionary exist. Here is an example of a dictionary, which puts each physics term next to its mathematical analogue:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zeidler |first=Eberhard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pk9yyC239scC |title=Quantum Field Theory II: Quantum Electrodynamics: A Bridge between Mathematicians and Physicists |date=2008-09-03 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-540-85377-0 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Original version for electromagnetism ===
[[File:AharonovBohmEffect.svg|thumb|Aharonov-Bohm experiment: electrons pass around a cylinder where there is a non-zero magnetic field. Outside the cylinder the field strength is 0.]]
Wu and Yang considered the description of an electron traveling around a cylinder in the presence of a magnetic field inside the cylinder (outside the cylinder the field vanishes i.e. <math>f_{\mu\nu}=0</math>). According to the [[Aharonov–Bohm effect]], the interference patterns shift by a factor <math>\exp(-i \Omega/\Omega_0)</math>, where <math>\Omega</math> is the magnetic flux and <math>\Omega_0</math> is the [[magnetic flux quantum]]. For two different fluxes ''a'' and ''b'', the results are identical if <math>\Omega_a-\Omega_b=N\Omega_0</math>, where <math>N</math> is an [[integer]]. We define the operator <math>S_{ab}</math> as the gauge transformation that brings the electron [[wave function]] from one configuration to the other <math>\psi_b=S_{ba}\psi_a</math>. For an electron that takes a path from point ''P'' to point ''Q'', we define the [[phase factor]] as 
:<math>\Phi_{QP} =\exp \left(-\frac{i}{\Omega_0} \int_P^Q A_\mu \mathrm{d} x^{\mu}\right) </math>, 
where <math>A_\mu</math> is the [[electromagnetic four-potential]]. For the case of a [[SU(2)]] gauge field, we can make the substitution
:<math>A_\mu=ib_\mu^kX_k</math>, 
where <math>X_k=-i\sigma_k/2</math> are the generators of SU(2), <math>\sigma_k</math> are the [[Pauli matrices]]. Under these concepts, Wu and Yang showed the relation between the language of gauge theory and [[Fiber bundle|fiber bundles]], was codified in following dictionary:<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Boi |first=Luciano |title=Geometrical and topological foundations of theoretical physics: from gauge theories to string program |journal=International Journal of Mathematics and Mathematical Sciences |year=2004 |language=en |volume=2004 |issue=34 |pages=1777–1836 |doi=10.1155/S0161171204304400 |issn=0161-1712|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Wells |first1=Raymond O'Neil |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e0MECAAAQBAJ |title=The Mathematical Heritage of Hermann Weyl |last2=Weyl |first2=Hermann |date=1988 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. |isbn=978-0-8218-1482-6 |language=en}}</ref>
